title: Space Exploration
seo_title: Grade 6 Science: Space Exploration Worksheets (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Describe technologies used to explore space, including Canadian contributions such as the Canadarm and Canadian astronauts; assess the benefits and costs of space exploration. (summary of the Ontario Science and Technology curriculum, 2022, Strand E: Earth and Space Systems – Space)
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 science worksheets on satellites, telescopes, rovers, the International Space Station, Canadarm and Canadian astronauts. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Satellites, telescopes, rovers and astronauts study space, and Canada has played a big part.
body_html:
How to think about it

People explore space with rockets, satellites, telescopes, rovers and astronauts.

  • Satellites give us weather forecasts, GPS and communications.
  • Canada built the Canadarm and Canadarm2; Canadian astronauts include Marc Garneau, Roberta Bondar, Chris Hadfield and Jeremy Hansen.
  • Space research gives inventions we use on Earth, but it costs a lot and leaves space junk.
Example

What is a satellite?

it orbits a planet

Answer: an object in orbit

Example

Why do astronauts exercise in space?

muscles and bones weaken without gravity's pull

Answer: to stay strong

Common mistakes

  • Thinking there is no gravity in space.
  • Thinking satellites stay still above Earth.
  • Thinking space exploration has no effect on daily life.

faq.q: How has Canada helped explore space?
faq.a: Canada built the Canadarm robotic arms, satellites like RADARSAT and parts of the James Webb Space Telescope, and has many astronauts.
They are falling around Earth at the same speed as the station, so they seem weightless.

faq.q: What are the costs of space exploration?
faq.a: It is very expensive, uses lots of fuel and adds space junk, so people discuss how to balance it with needs on Earth.

items.q: Why do stars look tiny?
c: They are smaller than the Moon.
items.e: Distance.

items.q: Priya asks: “Why are planets round?”
c: Gravity pulls their material toward the centre from all sides.
items.e: Large bodies become round.

items.q: What is space junk?
c: old satellites and pieces of rockets orbiting Earth
items.e: It can hit working satellites.

items.q: Aiden asks: “If a planet stopped moving forward, what would the Sun's gravity do?”
c: pull it straight toward the Sun
keep it in the same orbit
items.e: An orbit needs both forward motion and gravity.

items.q: What is the name of our galaxy?
items.e: A spiral galaxy.

items.q: What is a light year?
c: a year on a light planet
the time it takes light to travel one year
the distance light travels in one year
items.e: A unit of distance.

items.q: Why are rockets launched with huge amounts of fuel?
c: Because space is full of air
They need a lot of thrust to escape Earth's gravity.
items.e: Leaving Earth takes a lot of energy.

items.q: Ava asks: “If the Sun's gravity suddenly disappeared, what would Earth do?”
c: move off in a straight line into space
items.e: Without gravity's pull, nothing would curve Earth's path (Newton's first law).

items.q: What is one cost of space exploration?
c: It is very expensive and uses a lot of fuel.
items.e: People debate how to spend the money.

items.q: Ava asks: “Why is the Sun at the centre of our solar system's orbits?”
c: It was placed there by Jupiter.
It has more than 99% of the solar system's mass, so its gravity dominates.
items.e: Mass determines gravity.

items.q: Why do astronauts wear space suits on a spacewalk?
c: to give air and protect them from extreme temperatures and radiation
items.e: Space has no air to breathe.

items.q: Leah asks: “What holds the stars of the Milky Way together?”
c: gravity, mostly from the galaxy's huge mass
items.e: Galaxies are held together by gravity.

items.q: Is the Sun the biggest star in the Universe?
c: No. Many stars are much bigger than the Sun.
items.e: The Sun is a medium-sized star.

items.q: Which instrument lets you see craters on the Moon from your backyard?
items.e: Telescopes make faraway things look closer.

items.q: Which is a use of artificial satellites?
c: weather forecasts, GPS and phone signals
items.e: Canada's RADARSAT satellites watch ice and forests.

items.q: Why do astronauts exercise every day on the space station?
c: Without Earth's pull, their muscles and bones get weaker.
items.e: Exercise keeps them healthy.

items.q: Jeremy Hansen is part of which NASA mission to fly around the Moon?
items.e: He is the first Canadian on a Moon mission.

items.q: What is a galaxy?
c: a huge group of billions of stars
items.e: We live in the Milky Way.

items.q: Noah asks: “What keeps the Moon in orbit around Earth?”
c: Earth's gravity pulling on the moving Moon
items.e: Gravity bends the Moon's path into a curve.

items.q: Which force keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
items.e: The Sun's huge mass pulls them.

items.q: What do rovers on Mars do?
c: drive on the surface and study rocks, soil and air
items.e: Rovers are robots controlled from Earth.

items.q: What is the Canadarm?
c: a robotic arm built in Canada and used on the space shuttle and space station
items.e: Canadarm2 is on the International Space Station.

items.q: A person stands in South America. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the centre of Earth, so arrow A (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: What does a space telescope like the James Webb Space Telescope do?
c: It sees faraway stars and galaxies without Earth's air in the way.
items.e: Canada built parts of the Webb telescope.

items.q: What is the International Space Station?
c: a rocket that goes to Mars
a science lab that orbits Earth with astronauts on board
items.e: Canada is one of its partners.

items.q: A person stands in Canada. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the centre of Earth, so arrow D (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: Which is closest to Earth?
items.e: The sun is our closest star.

items.q: A person stands in Antarctica. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the centre of Earth, so arrow B (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: A star looks very dim from Earth. Which could be true?
c: It must not give off light.
It must be smaller than a house.
It may be very far away.
items.e: Distance can make even a very bright star look dim.

items.q: Which technology from space research is used on Earth?
items.e: Many inventions came from space research.

items.q: A person stands at the North Pole. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the centre of Earth, so arrow C (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: Who was the first Canadian to command the International Space Station?
items.e: He commanded it in 2013.

items.q: What is a light-year?
c: the time it takes to see a star
the distance light travels in one year
items.e: A light-year is a distance: about 9.5 trillion kilometres.

items.q: Which object in the sky is a star?
items.e: The moon and planets reflect sunlight. The sun makes its own light.

items.q: How does distance change how bright a light looks?
c: The farther away, the dimmer it looks.
The farther away, the brighter it looks.
Lights look brightest from very far away.
items.e: Light spreads out as it travels, so less reaches your eyes from far away.

items.q: Why does the sun look much brighter than other stars?
c: It is much closer to Earth than any other star.
It is the only star that gives off light.
Other stars are turned off in the day.
items.e: The sun is about 150 million km away. The next closest star is about 270 000 times farther.

items.q: A person stands at a place on the right side of Earth. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the centre of Earth, so arrow C (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: Why can't we see stars during the day?
c: The sun's bright light hides their dimmer light.
Stars move away during the day.
items.e: The stars are still there. Sunlight scattered in the sky outshines them.

items.q: Which statement about stars is true?
c: Many stars are as big as or bigger than the sun.
Stars are closer than the moon.
Stars are holes in the sky.
All stars are smaller than Earth.
items.e: Stars look like tiny dots only because they are so far away.

items.q: How did many Indigenous Peoples use the night sky?
c: to tell time, find directions and mark seasons
items.e: Star knowledge is passed down through stories.

items.q: Gravitational field strength on Mars is 3.7 N/kg. What is the weight there of an object with a mass of 50 kg?
items.e: weight = mass × g = 50 × 3.7 = 185 N.

items.q: Two children drop a ball at the same time: one in Canada and one at a place on the right side of Earth. Which way does each one fall?
c: Both fall toward the centre of Earth.
Both fall toward the bottom of the page.
One falls up and one falls down.
items.e: Down is toward Earth's centre everywhere, so both objects fall toward the ground under their feet.

items.q: What is a satellite?
c: an object that orbits a planet
items.e: The Moon is a natural satellite.

items.q: On Mars (g = 3.7 N/kg), Liam's backpack weighs 296 N. What is its mass?
items.e: mass = weight ÷ g = 296 ÷ 3.7 = 80 kg.

items.q: Who was the first Canadian in space?
items.e: He flew in 1984.

items.q: Why do astronauts float on the space station?
c: There is no gravity in space at all.
They and the station are falling around Earth together.
items.e: They are in constant free fall.

items.q: Two children drop a rock at the same time: one at the North Pole and one at a place on the right side of Earth. Which way does each one fall?
c: Both fall toward the bottom of the page.
One falls up and one falls down.
Both fall toward the centre of Earth.
items.e: Down is toward Earth's centre everywhere, so both objects fall toward the ground under their feet.

items.q: Gravitational field strength on Jupiter is 25 N/kg. What is the weight there of an object with a mass of 80 kg?
items.e: weight = mass × g = 80 × 25 = 2000 N.

items.q: In Ethan's model, a star has 3 times the mass of the Sun. A planet orbits it at the same distance as Earth. How does the pull on the planet compare with the Sun's pull on Earth (if the planets have equal mass)?
items.e: Gravity is proportional to mass.

items.q: In Chloe's model, a planet moves to 4 times its distance from the Sun. What happens to the Sun's pull on it?
items.e: Gravity weakens with the square of distance: 4² = 16.

items.q: Two children drop a ball at the same time: one at the South Pole and one at the North Pole. Which way does each one fall?
c: One falls up and one falls down.
Both fall toward the bottom of the page.
Both fall toward the centre of Earth.
items.e: Down is toward Earth's centre everywhere, so both objects fall toward the ground under their feet.

items.q: In Maya's model, a star has 4 times the mass of the Sun. A planet orbits it at the same distance as Earth. How does the pull on the planet compare with the Sun's pull on Earth (if the planets have equal mass)?
items.e: Gravity is proportional to mass.

items.q: In Benjamin's model, a planet moves to 2 times its distance from the Sun. What happens to the Sun's pull on it?
items.e: Gravity weakens with the square of distance: 2² = 4.

items.q: In Maya's model, a planet moves to 3 times its distance from the Sun. What happens to the Sun's pull on it?
items.e: Gravity weakens with the square of distance: 3² = 9.

items.q: On the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg), Maya's backpack weighs 72 N. What is its mass?
items.e: mass = weight ÷ g = 72 ÷ 1.6 = 45 kg.

items.q: Two children drop a cup at the same time: one at a place on the right side of Earth and one in South America. Which way does each one fall?
c: Both fall toward the centre of Earth.
Both fall toward the bottom of the page.
One falls up and one falls down.
items.e: Down is toward Earth's centre everywhere, so both objects fall toward the ground under their feet.

items.q: In Arjun's model, a star has 2 times the mass of the Sun. A planet orbits it at the same distance as Earth. How does the pull on the planet compare with the Sun's pull on Earth (if the planets have equal mass)?
items.e: Gravity is proportional to mass.

items.q: On the Earth (g = 10 N/kg), Noah's backpack weighs 450 N. What is its mass?
items.e: mass = weight ÷ g = 450 ÷ 10 = 45 kg.

items.q: Two children drop a cup at the same time: one on a ship at sea and one at the North Pole. Which way does each one fall?
c: One falls up and one falls down.
Both fall toward the centre of Earth.
Both fall toward the bottom of the page.
items.e: Down is toward Earth's centre everywhere, so both objects fall toward the ground under their feet.

items.q: Gravitational field strength on Mars is 3.7 N/kg. What is the weight there of an object with a mass of 80 kg?
items.e: weight = mass × g = 80 × 3.7 = 296 N.

items.q: What is mass?
c: the force of gravity on it
the amount of matter in an object
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: Why do astronauts weigh less on the Moon?
c: The Moon's gravity is weaker because it has less mass than the Earth.
There is no gravity on the Moon.
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: What shape are most planetary orbits?
items.e: Slightly stretched circles.

items.q: What is the gravitational field strength on the Earth?
items.e: More precisely 9.8 N/kg.

items.q: What is a galaxy?
c: a huge system of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity
items.e: The Milky Way has hundreds of billions of stars.

items.q: What keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth?
c: the gravitational pull of the Earth
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: Which planet takes the shortest time to orbit the Sun?
items.e: It is closest: about 88 days.

items.q: What does the size of gravitational attraction between two objects depend on?
c: their masses and the distance between them
items.e: More mass, closer: stronger.

items.q: What unit is mass measured in?
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: What two things make an orbit?
c: forward motion and gravity pulling toward the centre
items.e: Gravity curves the path.

items.q: Which object has the strongest gravity in our solar system?
items.e: It has the most mass.

items.q: What unit is weight measured in?
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: What is a galaxy?
c: a huge group of billions of stars held together by gravity
items.e: We live in the Milky Way.

items.q: Is there gravity in space?
c: No, there is none at all.
Yes. Gravity acts everywhere, getting weaker with distance.
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: Does Earth's gravity reach the Moon?
c: No, it stops at the atmosphere.
Yes. It keeps the Moon in orbit.
items.e: Gravity reaches far into space.

items.q: Why do outer planets take longer to orbit the Sun?
c: They travel a longer path and move more slowly because the Sun's pull is weaker.
items.e: Distance matters.

items.q: What is weight?
c: the amount of matter in an object
the force of gravity on an object
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: What is the Sun?
items.e: Our nearest star.

items.q: Which quantity stays the same on the Moon as on the Earth: mass or weight?
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: What is 1 astronomical unit (AU)?
c: the average distance from Earth to the Sun, about 150 million km
items.e: Used for solar system distances.

items.q: If the Earth's axis were not tilted, what would happen?
c: There would be no day and night.
Summer would last all year everywhere.
There would be almost no seasons.
items.e: Tilt causes seasons.

items.q: Why would you weigh less on the Moon than on Earth?
c: The Moon's gravity is weaker because it has less mass.
Your mass is less on the Moon.
The Moon is closer to the Sun.
There is no gravity on the Moon.
items.e: Weight depends on gravity.

items.q: Which evidence best supports the claim: “Gravity pulls water down.”
c: Every dropped object in the class test fell to the floor, no matter where it was dropped.
Plumb lines all over the world hang toward Earth's centre.
Rivers flow from mountains down to the sea.
A spring scale stretches when an object hangs from it.
items.e: This observation directly shows that gravity pulls water down.

items.q: Chloe's model shows a cloud of gas and dust shrinking and spinning faster. What forms at the centre?
items.e: Most mass collects at the centre.

items.q: When we look at a star 100 light years away, what are we seeing?
c: light that left the star 100 years ago
the star as it is right now
items.e: Looking back in time.

items.q: Why should students repeat a drop test several times?
c: to make sure the results are reliable
items.e: Repeated trials show whether the result happens every time.

items.q: Zoe throws a ball forward. Which force makes it curve toward the ground?
items.e: Her throw moves it forward; gravity pulls it down, so its path curves.

items.q: Which is the best way to show a younger student that “down” is toward Earth's centre?
c: Drop a ball in the classroom only.
Draw an arrow to the bottom of a map.
Put toy figures all around a globe and point each one's arrow into the globe.
items.e: A globe model shows that down points to the centre from every place.

items.q: Ethan measures that a ball dropped from 2 metres takes a little more than half a second to fall. What would happen if he did this in a different country?
c: It would not fall at all.
It would fall about the same way, toward the ground there.
items.e: Gravity works the same way everywhere on Earth's surface.

items.q: Which evidence best supports the claim: “All objects fall toward the ground when dropped.”
c: Every dropped object in the class test fell to the floor, no matter where it was dropped.
A ball falls even though nothing touches it.
Plumb lines all over the world hang toward Earth's centre.
A spring scale stretches when an object hangs from it.
items.e: This observation directly shows that all objects fall toward the ground when dropped.

items.q: Ava swings a ball on a string in a circle. In her model, what does the string represent?
c: the Sun's gravity pulling the planet inward
items.e: Gravity is the inward pull.

items.q: Zoe wants to test whether the height of a ramp changes how fast a car rolls down. What should she keep the same?
c: only the colour of the car
the car and the length and surface of the ramp
items.e: Only the height changes, so the test is fair.

items.q: Which evidence best supports the claim: “Gravity pulls toward Earth's centre.”
c: Every dropped object in the class test fell to the floor, no matter where it was dropped.
Plumb lines all over the world hang toward Earth's centre.
Rivers flow from mountains down to the sea.
A ball falls even though nothing touches it.
items.e: This observation directly shows that gravity pulls toward Earth's centre.

items.q: Mateo drops two balls of the same size: a golf ball and a ping-pong ball, from 1 metre. They land at almost the same time. What does this show?
c: Gravity makes objects fall at about the same rate when air resistance is small.
Gravity does not affect light objects.
Heavier objects always fall much faster.
items.e: The pull of gravity speeds up all objects in the same way. Air resistance makes only a small difference here.

items.q: Why would a spacecraft need more speed to orbit close to Jupiter than close to the Moon?
c: Jupiter's much larger mass pulls harder.
Jupiter is closer to the Sun.
items.e: More mass, more speed needed.

items.q: Which model best describes the solar system?
c: planets orbiting the Sun, held by the Sun's gravity
items.e: Sun-centered model.

items.q: Which evidence best supports the claim: “Objects have weight because of gravity.”
c: Rivers flow from mountains down to the sea.
A spring scale stretches when an object hangs from it.
A ball falls even though nothing touches it.
Plumb lines all over the world hang toward Earth's centre.
items.e: This observation directly shows that objects have weight because of gravity.

items.q: Noah hangs a weight on a string and holds it still. Which direction does the string point?
items.e: The weight pulls the string in the direction of gravity.

items.q: Noah lets go of the string while the ball is swinging. What does the ball do, and what does it model?
c: It flies off in a straight line, like a planet without gravity.
It falls straight down to the centre.
items.e: No inward pull, no curve.

items.q: Why do astronomers use light years and not kilometres?
c: The distances are so huge that kilometres give enormous numbers.
Kilometres do not work in space.
It is a rule from the Moon.
items.e: Convenient units.
